Examples like this show how broken and unreliable human convictions are. All human brains are at risk for all sorts of cognitive errors and biases that allow them to gain strong convictions in propositions that are so non-trivial that no longer believing in them could be worldview shattering yet don't seem to be rationally justified to an impartial person.

The problem is that we can often see this in others very clearly but have a lot of trouble in applying an impartial look at our own worldview. For example there are billions of religious people that can easily tell you how wrong and deluded members of other religions are (and even different sects of their own religion) but seem baffled that others think their own fantastical religious/metaphysical worldviews are deluded.

Critical thinking, rather than intuitive thinking, is not the norm; it is basically an emergent series of software patches that helps bring to the surface our patterns of thought and see if they are indeed coherent. We should perhaps strive best to think critically about plausibility and probability and be very cautious of propositions (whether from oneself or another) that come with very strong convictions that don't seem to straightforwardly hold up as rationally justified to an ideal impartial person. It is okay not to know, and it isn't a virtue to fudge details and bullshit yourself and others to make up for actual gaps in knowledge and lack of certainty.

The blockchain itself is a decentralized ledger. Here is what you need to understand what that means:

This "ledger" is a wallet, which contains a cryptographic hash which can be broken down into two parts, a "private" key (think like a password only you have) which pairs with "public keys". Through your wallet, you secure it with ownership of the private key, and the private key is part of a key-pair for the public keys. Giving someone access to your private key is, in essence, giving them access to your entire wallet including all public keys you have ever generated.

Through your wallet, you can generate as many public keys as you wish, all unlocked with your private key, allowing you to make a new wallet address for literally every single transaction you do which cannot truly be traced back to you because only you have the private key. It would be like having a bank account with Chase, but having a different 16 digit credit card transaction for each and every transaction you make - Chase is the only "authority" that can see all of those card numbers are you, in the same way that your private key, which only you have, is the authority that all of the public wallet ID's are you. Ergo, if you generate new public keys for say every exchange you use, and every transaction you do with another individual's wallet, you have in essence become anonymous because nobody but you, or someone with your private key, can ever associate one public transaction to another. Most people are somewhat lazy and use the same or a set of public keys for more than one source, which would allow some degree of rudimentary "tracking", but even this isn't absolute.

The blockchain is "Decentralized" in the sense that it is not validated by one absolute authority. Once again, all the purchases you make with Chase are validated by Chase. Chase determines your account balance. Chase does the math for your debits and credits, and Chase has the ability to, arbitrarily with nothing more than the manipulation of computer code, either zero out your entire balance or claim you owe millions.

The blockchain has no central authority, because each transaction you do is compiled into a list of transactions. Every block reward (so, in the case of Bitcoin, every 10 minutes - it varies coin by coin) solves a complex math problem and does two things:

1) Rewards the selected miner with a block reward, which is a motivation for miners to mine as it generates a set amount of the currency for their effort. 2) Compiles a list of all transactions performed in since the last block and distributes them as the aforementioned decentralized problem "solution" to all other wallets.

This means that every single person with a wallet sees your "public key" transactions happened, and everyone has validation of the exchange of the cryptographic currency in their wallets. Everyone's wallets must match, so you cannot cheat this system by lying about a transaction, or just doing what banks do and punching in a few keys into a computer which adjusts a table on a SQL database and changes your bank account balance through credits and debits. And, since nobody has your "private" key, nobody knows those transactions are you, except you.

In short, the blockchain is a decentralized ledger with built in capacity to anonymize literally every single transaction you do (if you take the time necessary to do so), in a system where there is no centralized authority so you cannot have a regulating body such as a government pass a law and then steal from your wallet without your permission, with block rewards given to those who participate in continuing the ledger forward every set validation. Because the transactions cannot be easily revoked, like say at credit card charge-back, there is significantly more personal education and precautions necessary for one to participate (which generally excludes those less informed, or those easily scammed, from having a positive experience with the technology).

With all of this said, the cryptographic coins exist in their own ecosystem, and many exchanges exist allowing individuals to translate one coin to another. This is the actual crypt-coin marketplace ecosystem - the translation to FIAT currency only exists because humans who are otherwise too lazy, incapable technically, or simply not interested in participating in the distributed "mining" aspect of solving the block rewards to update the ledger still need a method to attain the coins themselves for their make-believe paper FIAT currency. Economics of supply and demand play a role here as there is generally less people selling coins than those looking to buy them, and as such the coin prices often increase exponentially - however they are so volatile that this increase could just as likely be a decrease, or the overall massive 2000% +/- swings you see in things like Bitcoin.

With only 4.2 million estimated unique individual users in some 2880+ known coins, the actual number of humans playing in this sandbox is staggeringly small compared to the number who want to participate, or who even KNOW about the cryptographic coins to begin with. Because of this, speculation on price fluctuation is rampant, and many less technically educated fall victim to constant scam coin pump and dumps, or coins with very large "pre-mines" given to developers before going public to the regular miners. The "Average Joe" often comes to me going "DID YOU HEAR HOW BITCOIN'S CEO SCAMMED PEOPLE?" everytime an Exchange gets hacked, because people continue to lack the understanding to realize that an Exchange should never hold any of the crypto-currency long-term to begin with, as the only security one will really have is an actual wallet on their personal systems, so the hurdles to leap over just to get started involve an extremely steep learning curve.
